title: Disparadores del Subjuntivo — Practice
description: Authored B1 practice set for choosing subjunctive vs indicative: WEIRDO triggers, always-subjunctive conjunctions, the time clauses that switch on future reference, and the same-subject infinitive rule.

lessons.summary: Forming the subjunctive is one skill; knowing when it is required is another. The subjunctive lives in a subordinate clause, normally after 'que', and normally when the subject changes: 'Quiero que vengas' — but with the same subject you use an infinitive instead: 'Quiero venir'. The classic trigger list is WEIRDO: Wishes (querer, esperar, preferir, ojalá), Emotions (alegrarse de, sentir, es una lástima), Impersonal expressions (es importante/necesario/posible/mejor), Recommendations and requests (pedir, sugerir, recomendar, aconsejar), Doubt and denial (dudar, no creer, no es verdad), Ojalá. The mirror image matters just as much: expressions of certainty take the INDICATIVE — creo que, es verdad que, es obvio que, sé que. Negate them and the subjunctive appears: 'Creo que viene' → 'No creo que venga'. Six conjunctions always take the subjunctive because what follows is by definition unrealised: para que, antes de que, sin que, a menos que, con tal de que, en caso de que. Time conjunctions (cuando, en cuanto, hasta que, después de que, mientras, tan pronto como) take the subjunctive only when they point at the future: 'Cuando llego a casa, ceno' (habit, indicative) vs 'Cuando llegue a casa, cenaré' (future, subjunctive). Finally, an adjective clause takes the subjunctive when its antecedent is indefinite or non-existent: 'Busco un piso que tenga balcón' (any such flat) vs 'Vivo en el piso que tiene balcón' (a specific one).

examples.spanish: Creo que viene. / No creo que venga.
examples.english: I think he's coming. / I don't think he's coming.
I want to go to the cinema.

examples.spanish: Te lo explico para que lo entiendas.
examples.english: I'm explaining it so that you understand it.

examples.spanish: Cuando llego a casa, siempre ceno.
examples.english: When I get home, I always have dinner.

examples.spanish: Cuando llegue a casa, te llamaré.

items.prompt: Es verdad que él ___ razón.
items.promptEnglish: It's true that he's right.
items.explanation: 'Es verdad que' asserts a certainty, so the indicative follows: tiene.

items.prompt: No es verdad que él ___ razón.
items.promptEnglish: It's not true that he's right.
items.explanation: Negating a certainty removes the assertion, so the subjunctive follows: tenga.

items.prompt: Creo que ella ___ hoy.
items.promptEnglish: I think she's coming today.
items.explanation: 'Creer que' in the affirmative expresses belief as fact → indicative: viene.

items.prompt: No creo que ella ___ hoy.
items.promptEnglish: I don't think she's coming today.
items.explanation: 'No creer que' expresses doubt → subjunctive: venga. This pair is the single most useful trigger contrast to memorise.

items.prompt: Es obvio que ___ cansado.
items.promptEnglish: It's obvious that you're tired.
items.explanation: Impersonal expressions of certainty (es obvio, es cierto, está claro) take the indicative.

items.prompt: Es importante que ___ temprano. (llegar, tú)
items.promptEnglish: It's important that you arrive early.
items.explanation: Impersonal expressions of value or need (importante, necesario, mejor, posible) take the subjunctive.

items.prompt: Cuando ___ a casa, siempre ceno con mi familia.
items.promptEnglish: When I get home, I always have dinner with my family.
items.explanation: 'Cuando' describing a habit or a completed fact takes the indicative.

items.prompt: Cuando ___ a casa, te llamaré.
items.promptEnglish: When I get home, I'll call you.
items.explanation: The same 'cuando' switches to the subjunctive when it points at an event that hasn't happened yet.

items.prompt: Te lo explico para que lo ___.
items.promptEnglish: I'm explaining it so that you understand it.
items.explanation: 'Para que' is always subjunctive — the purpose hasn't been realised yet.

items.prompt: Quiero ___ al cine esta noche. (yo quiero, yo voy)
items.promptEnglish: I want to go to the cinema tonight.
items.explanation: With no change of subject there is no 'que' clause — use the plain infinitive: Quiero ir.

items.prompt: Quiero que tú ___ al cine conmigo.
items.promptEnglish: I want you to come to the cinema with me.
items.explanation: The subject changes (yo → tú), so 'querer que' + subjunctive: vayas.

items.prompt: Me alegro de que ___ aquí. (estar, tú)
items.promptEnglish: I'm glad you're here.
items.explanation: Emotion triggers (alegrarse de, sentir, temer) take the subjunctive even though the fact is real.

items.prompt: Busco un apartamento que ___ balcón. (cualquiera con balcón)
items.promptEnglish: I'm looking for a flat with a balcony.
items.explanation: The flat is indefinite — it may not exist yet — so the adjective clause takes the subjunctive.

items.prompt: Vivo en el apartamento que ___ balcón. (uno concreto)
items.promptEnglish: I live in the flat that has a balcony.
items.explanation: A specific, known flat → indicative. Compare with the indefinite version.

items.prompt: Aunque ___ caro, lo compraré. ('even if' — no sé el precio)
items.promptEnglish: Even if it's expensive, I'll buy it.
items.explanation: 'Aunque' + subjunctive = 'even if' (hypothetical). 'Aunque es caro' would mean 'even though it IS expensive' — a known fact.

items.prompt: Antes de que ___, apaga la luz. (salir, tú)
items.promptEnglish: Before you leave, turn off the light.
items.explanation: 'Antes de que' is always subjunctive.

items.prompt: No saldremos a menos que ___ de llover. (parar)
items.promptEnglish: We won't go out unless it stops raining.
items.explanation: 'A menos que' is always subjunctive.

items.prompt: Te ayudo sin que me lo ___. (pedir, tú)
items.promptEnglish: I help you without you asking me to.
items.explanation: 'Sin que' is always subjunctive.

items.prompt: Lleva paraguas en caso de que ___. (llover)
items.promptEnglish: Take an umbrella in case it rains.
items.explanation: 'En caso de que' is always subjunctive.

items.prompt: Ojalá que ___ sol mañana. (hacer)
items.promptEnglish: Hopefully it'll be sunny tomorrow.
items.explanation: 'Ojalá' always takes the subjunctive — it is a wish, never a statement.

items.prompt: Mi madre me pide que la ___ más a menudo. (llamar, yo)
items.promptEnglish: My mother asks me to call her more often.
items.explanation: Requests (pedir que, rogar que) take the subjunctive.

items.prompt: Te recomiendo que ___ ese libro. (leer, tú)
items.promptEnglish: I recommend you read that book.
items.explanation: Recommendations (recomendar, sugerir, aconsejar) take the subjunctive.

items.prompt: Es posible que ellos no ___ nada. (saber)
items.promptEnglish: It's possible they don't know anything.
items.explanation: 'Es posible que' expresses uncertainty → subjunctive. Note 'es probable que' behaves the same way.

items.prompt: Te llamaré en cuanto ___ la respuesta. (tener, yo)
items.promptEnglish: I'll call you as soon as I have the answer.
items.explanation: 'En cuanto' pointing at a future event → subjunctive.

items.prompt: Esperaré aquí hasta que ___. (volver, tú)
items.promptEnglish: I'll wait here until you come back.
items.explanation: 'Hasta que' with a future reference → subjunctive.

items.prompt: Es una lástima que no ___ venir. (poder, tú)
items.promptEnglish: It's a shame you can't come.
items.explanation: Emotional reactions take the subjunctive: es una lástima que + puedas.

items.prompt: Dudo que ___ tiempo para todo. (haber)
items.promptEnglish: I doubt there's time for everything.
items.explanation: 'Dudar que' → subjunctive. Impersonal haber becomes haya.

items.prompt: Negate the trigger: "Es cierto que estudia mucho" → "No es cierto que ___ mucho."
items.promptEnglish: It's not true that he studies a lot.
items.explanation: Negating the certainty flips the clause to the subjunctive: estudia → estudie.

items.prompt: Negate the trigger: "Creo que tiene razón" → "No creo que ___ razón."
items.promptEnglish: I don't think he's right.
items.explanation: creo que + indicative → no creo que + subjunctive: tiene → tenga.

items.prompt: Escribe dos frases sobre el mismo tema: una que empiece con "Creo que…" y otra con "No creo que…".
items.promptEnglish: Write two sentences on the same subject: one starting "Creo que…" and one starting "No creo que…".
items.guidance: Must contain two sentences. The 'Creo que…' sentence must use the INDICATIVE (e.g. 'Creo que va a llover') and the 'No creo que…' sentence must use the SUBJUNCTIVE (e.g. 'No creo que vaya a llover'). Mark incorrect if either clause uses the wrong mood, or if only one sentence is given.
items.sampleAnswer: Creo que mañana hace calor. No creo que mañana haga frío.
items.explanation: Affirmative certainty takes the indicative; negated certainty takes the subjunctive.
